title: Sprint 3 — Build a Task Manager App (HTML + CSS + JS + localStorage)
description: Build a complete, fully interactive Task Manager web app from scratch. Users can add tasks, mark them as complete, delete them, and filter by status — and everything persists in localStorage so no data is lost on refresh. This sprint covers DOM manipulation, event handling, dynamic rendering, and browser storage.

tickets.title: Ticket 1 — HTML Structure & CSS Base Styles
tickets.description: Build the complete HTML skeleton and base CSS for the task manager. No JavaScript yet — focus on getting the structure and look right so the app feels polished before it becomes interactive.

tasks.title: Task 1 — App HTML Structure
tasks.description:
Create `index.html` with the following structure inside `<body>`:
- A `<header>` with an `<h1>` (app name, e.g. 'TaskFlow')
- A `<main>` containing:
  - A `<form id="taskForm">` with: an `<input type="text" id="taskInput" placeholder="Add a new task...">` and a `<button type="submit">Add Task</button>`
  - A filter bar `<div class="filters">` with 3 `<button>` elements: data-filter="all", data-filter="active", data-filter="completed"
  - An empty `<ul id="taskList">` where tasks will be rendered
  - A `<div class="task-stats">` showing a `<span id="taskCount">` and a 'Clear Completed' `<button id="clearCompleted">`
- A `<footer>` with a copyright line
- Link `style.css` and `script.js`

tasks.title: Task 2 — Full App Styling
tasks.description:
Style the app completely in `style.css` so it looks like a real product:
- Centred layout, max-width ~600px, card-style container with shadow and border-radius
- Custom colour scheme using `:root` CSS variables
- The form input and button side-by-side using Flexbox
- Filter buttons: horizontal row, the active filter button should have a distinct `background` or `border` style (use a `.active` class)
- Task list items (`<li>`) styled as rows with: checkbox on the left, task text in the middle, delete button on the right
- Completed tasks should have `text-decoration: line-through` and muted text colour
- Smooth `transition` on all hover and state changes

tickets.title: Ticket 2 — Core Task Logic (Add, Complete, Delete)
tickets.description: Wire up the core interactivity of the task manager. Users can add new tasks, mark them as done by clicking a checkbox, and delete individual tasks. Each action must update the displayed task count.

tasks.title: Task 1 — Add Tasks & Render List
tasks.description: It's time to bring the Task Manager to life in `script.js`. First, initialize an empty array called `tasks` to hold all your task objects. Next, set up an event listener on the form (`#taskForm`) for the `submit` event. Inside the listener, call `e.preventDefault()` so the page doesn't reload. Grab the value from the input field, and if it's not empty, create a new task object like `{ id: Date.now(), text: inputValue, completed: false }`. Push this object into your `tasks` array, clear the input field, and finally, call a new function named `renderTasks()`. In your `renderTasks()` function, clear the `#taskList` innerHTML, loop through the `tasks` array, and create a new `<li>` for each task containing a checkbox, a span for the text, and a delete button. Append each `<li>` to the `#taskList`. Lastly, write an `updateCount()` function to count how many tasks are not completed, and update the text inside `#taskCount`.

tasks.title: Task 2 — Toggle Complete & Delete
tasks.description: Now add the ability to mark tasks as done and delete them. In your `renderTasks()` function, when you create the checkbox for a task, add a `change` event listener to it. When triggered, find that specific task by its `id` in the `tasks` array and flip its `completed` boolean. Then, call `renderTasks()` again to update the UI. To show a task is completed, conditionally add a `completed` CSS class to the `<li>` if `task.completed` is true. For the delete button, add a `click` event listener that filters the `tasks` array to remove the task with the matching `id`, and then calls `renderTasks()` again. Make sure your `updateCount()` runs at the end of `renderTasks()` so the remaining task count is always accurate.

tickets.title: Ticket 3 — Filters, Clear Completed & localStorage
tickets.description: Complete the app with filter functionality (All / Active / Completed), a 'Clear Completed' button, and full localStorage persistence so the task list survives a page refresh.

tasks.title: Task 1 — Filter Buttons
tasks.description: Let's make the filter buttons work. Create a variable `currentFilter` initialized to `'all'`. Add click event listeners to all three `.filter-btn` buttons. When a button is clicked, set `currentFilter` to the button's `data-filter` value, remove the `active` class from all buttons, and add it to the clicked button. Then, call `renderTasks()`. Now, update your `renderTasks()` function: before looping over the `tasks` array, filter it based on `currentFilter`. If it's `'active'`, only render tasks where `completed` is false. If it's `'completed'`, only render tasks where `completed` is true. The task count at the bottom should still always show the number of active tasks, regardless of which filter is currently selected.

tasks.title: Task 2 — Clear Completed & localStorage Persistence
tasks.description: Finally, add the clear completed button and local storage persistence so users don't lose their data when they refresh the page. Add a click event listener to the `#clearCompleted` button that filters out all completed tasks from the `tasks` array and then calls `renderTasks()`. For persistence, write a `saveTasks()` function that takes the `tasks` array, converts it to a string using `JSON.stringify()`, and saves it to `localStorage.setItem('taskflow_tasks', ...)`. Call `saveTasks()` every time the `tasks` array changes (on add, toggle, delete, and clear). Then, write a `loadTasks()` function that reads from `localStorage` when the page first loads, parses the string back into an array with `JSON.parse()`, and assigns it to `tasks`. Run `loadTasks()` and `renderTasks()` at the very bottom of your script so the app starts up with the saved data.
